questions.question: Who among the following is the founder of the Vrindavan Gurukul in Mumbai and Vrindavan Gurukul in Bhubaneshwar?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Hariprasad Chaurasia**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Hariprasad Chaurasia**, a renowned Indian flutist, is credited with establishing the Vrindavan Gurukul in Mumbai and Bhubaneshwar.
 
• The Vrindavan Gurukul is a center dedicated to teaching and preserving the art of Indian classical music, especially the **bansuri (bamboo flute)**.
 
• Hariprasad Chaurasia follows the **Guru-Shishya Parampara** (teacher-student tradition) at the Gurukul, where students live and learn under his guidance.
 
• The Gurukuls were set up to provide a serene environment for learning Indian classical music away from urban distractions.
 
• Both Mumbai and Bhubaneshwar centers are known for nurturing talented musicians and preserving India's rich musical heritage.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Hariprasad Chaurasia**

 
 
• He is one of the most celebrated flutists in Indian classical music and a recipient of numerous awards, including the **Padma Bhushan (1992)** and **Padma Vibhushan (2000)**.
 
• His music is rooted in the **Hindustani classical tradition**, and he is known for his unique playing style.
 
• Hariprasad Chaurasia has collaborated with international artists and contributed to globalizing Indian classical music.
 
 
 
• **Guru-Shishya Parampara**
 
 
• This is an ancient Indian tradition of teaching where students (shishya) learn under the close guidance of a master (guru).
 
• It emphasizes a holistic approach to learning, including discipline, devotion, and practice.
 
• It is widely followed in Indian classical music, dance, and other traditional art forms.
 
 
 
• **Bansuri**
 
 
• The bansuri is a traditional Indian bamboo flute associated with Lord Krishna in Indian mythology.
 
• It is a key instrument in Hindustani classical music and is known for its melodious and soulful sound.
 
• Hariprasad Chaurasia is credited with elevating the bansuri to the status of a major instrument in Indian classical music.
 
 
 
• **Indian Classical Music**
 
 
• Indian classical music is divided into two traditions: **Hindustani (North Indian) and Carnatic (South Indian)**.
 
• It is based on ragas (melodic frameworks) and talas (rhythmic cycles).
 
• Indian classical music has a rich history and is deeply intertwined with spirituality and cultural traditions.

questions.question: In 1889, ________ established the Mukti Mission, in Pune, a refuge for young widows who had been deserted and abused by their families.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Pandita Ramabai**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Pandita Ramabai** was a renowned social reformer and educationist in India, particularly known for her efforts in women's emancipation.
 
• She established the **Mukti Mission** in 1889 in Pune, Maharashtra, as a refuge for young widows who faced desertion and abuse.
 
• The Mukti Mission provided widows with shelter, education, and vocational training, aiming to help them achieve self-reliance.
 
• Ramabai was a pioneer in advocating for the rights of women, especially widows, during a time when they faced severe social stigma and hardships.
 
• She was also an accomplished scholar of Sanskrit and a key figure in the 19th-century Indian social reform movement.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Widowhood in 19th-Century India:**

 
 
• Widows during this period were often ostracized, deprived of property rights, and subjected to severe societal discrimination.
 
• Social reformers like Pandita Ramabai sought to challenge these oppressive customs and provide avenues for widows to rebuild their lives.
 
 
 
• **Mukti Mission:**
 
 
• Initially started as a shelter for young widows, it later expanded into a broader initiative for women's empowerment.
 
• The Mission provided education, healthcare, and skill development, fostering independence among its residents.
 
 
 
• **Pandita Ramabai’s Legacy:**
 
 
• She was honored with the title "Pandita" due to her profound knowledge of Sanskrit and religious texts.
 
• Her autobiography, *My Testimony*, and other writings highlighted the plight of Indian women and advocated social reform.
 
 
 
• **Other Social Reformers of the Era:**
 
 
• Raja Ram Mohan Roy and Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar were among her contemporaries who worked to abolish harmful practices like Sati and child marriage.
 
• The Brahmo Samaj, Arya Samaj, and similar movements played a key role in shaping 19th-century social reforms.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT an objective of the Fundamental Rights which are mentioned in the Indian Constitution?

options.text: Promote the ideal of political democracy
Prevent the establishment of an authoritarian and despotic rule
Establish a government of laws and not of men
Drive the citizens towards the objectives of the government

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Drive the citizens towards the objectives of the government**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Fundamental Rights enshrined in the Indian Constitution aim to promote individual liberty and equality, safeguarding citizens from state excesses.
 
• They are designed to establish a framework for political democracy by guaranteeing civil liberties to all citizens.
 
• One major objective is to prevent the establishment of authoritarian or despotic rule by ensuring checks on the powers of the state.
 
• The principle of "a government of laws and not of men" is upheld by the Fundamental Rights, ensuring the rule of law in governance.
 
• However, Fundamental Rights do not aim to "drive citizens towards the objectives of the government," as their primary purpose is to protect citizens' rights and freedoms, not to enforce state-driven goals.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Fundamental Rights in the Indian Constitution:**

 
 
• Enshrined in Part III of the Constitution (Articles 12-35).
 
• They are classified into six categories: Right to Equality, Right to Freedom, Right against Exploitation, Right to Freedom of Religion, Cultural and Educational Rights, and Right to Constitutional Remedies.
 
• They are enforceable by the courts, and citizens can approach the judiciary in case of violation.
 
 
 
• **Rule of Law:**
 
 
• A fundamental principle that emphasizes the supremacy of law over arbitrary powers.
 
• It ensures that all individuals, including government officials, are subject to the law.
 
 
 
• **Importance of Preventing Authoritarian Rule:**
 
 
• Fundamental Rights act as a safeguard against the concentration of power in the hands of the state or individuals.
 
• They promote democratic values by ensuring accountability, transparency, and citizen participation.
 
 
 
• **Right to Constitutional Remedies:**
 
 
• Considered the "heart and soul" of the Indian Constitution, as described by Dr. B.R. Ambedkar.
 
• Allows citizens to approach the Supreme Court or High Courts to enforce Fundamental Rights through writs like Habeas Corpus, Mandamus, Prohibition, Certiorari, and Quo Warranto.

questions.question: The tribal dance Daang is associated with which Indian state?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Gujarat**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Daang** is a tribal dance form performed primarily in the **Dang district of Gujarat**, which is home to various tribal communities.
 
• This dance is associated with celebrations, festivals, and community gatherings of the tribal groups in the region.
 
• The performers of Daang wear traditional tribal attire, which often includes vibrant and colorful clothing, along with accessories made from natural materials.
 
• Musical instruments such as **drums and flutes** are commonly used to accompany the dance, creating a rhythmic and lively atmosphere.
 
• The dance reflects the cultural heritage and the close connection of the tribal communities with nature and their surroundings.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Dang district:**

 
 
• Located in the southern part of Gujarat, the Dang district is known for its dense forests, tribal population, and natural beauty.
 
• The name "Dang" is derived from the Dangi tribes, who are the indigenous inhabitants of the region.
 
 
 
• **Tribal culture in Gujarat:**
 
 
• Gujarat has a rich tribal culture, with major tribes including Bhils, Rathwas, Garasias, and Dangis.
 
• These tribes have unique languages, traditions, and art forms, including dance, music, and crafts.
 
 
 
• **Significance of tribal dances:**
 
 
• Tribal dances like Daang are not just entertainment but are deeply rooted in spiritual and social traditions.
 
• They are performed during festivals, harvests, and religious ceremonies, symbolizing unity and cultural identity.
 
 
 
• **Preservation of tribal art forms:**
 
 
• Efforts are being made by the government and NGOs to document and preserve tribal dance forms like Daang to promote cultural heritage.
 
• Such initiatives include organizing tribal festivals and cultural exchange programs.

questions.question: Due to the need for irrigation facilities and pesticides/fertilisers, the first phase of the Green Revolution benefitted few affluent states such as _____________.

options.text: Punjab, Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu
Punjab, Andhra Pradesh and Uttar Pradesh
Punjab, Arunachal Pradesh and Uttar Pradesh

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Punjab, Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The first phase of the Green Revolution in India (1960s-70s) focused on improving agricultural productivity through **high-yield variety (HYV) seeds, irrigation, and chemical fertilizers.**
 
• States like **Punjab, Andhra Pradesh, and Tamil Nadu** benefitted the most due to better access to irrigation facilities and agricultural infrastructure.
 
• **Punjab** emerged as the leader in wheat production, while **Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu** excelled in rice production during this period.
 
• The revolution primarily favored regions with well-established irrigation systems, leaving rain-fed and economically weaker states behind.
 
• This phase contributed significantly to India’s food security but also led to economic disparities between regions.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Green Revolution:**

 
 
• An agricultural reform initiative in the 1960s aimed at increasing food grain production, particularly wheat and rice, using modern techniques.
 
• Introduced by Dr. Norman Borlaug globally and spearheaded in India by Dr. M.S. Swaminathan.
 
• Key components included high-yield variety seeds, chemical fertilizers, pesticides, and improved irrigation.
 
 
 
• **Impact on Punjab:**
 
 
• Punjab became the "Granary of India" due to the adoption of Green Revolution techniques.
 
• Widespread use of tube wells and canals boosted irrigation, leading to a sharp rise in wheat production.
 
 
 
• **Challenges:**
 
 
• Over-dependence on chemical fertilizers led to soil degradation.
 
• Water-intensive crops like rice caused groundwater depletion in states like Punjab and Tamil Nadu.
 
• Uneven benefits created regional and class-based disparities in agricultural development.
 
 
 
• **Second Phase of the Green Revolution:**
 
 
• Launched in the 1980s to address regional imbalances by focusing on eastern and rain-fed states like Bihar, Odisha, and West Bengal.
 
• Emphasized sustainable agricultural practices, including diversification and water management.

questions.question: The brittle crust and the top part of the upper mantle of the earth is called:
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**lithosphere**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The lithosphere is the **brittle outer layer** of Earth, consisting of the crust and the uppermost mantle.
 
• It is divided into tectonic plates that float on the underlying semi-fluid asthenosphere.
 
• The lithosphere is generally **rigid and solid**, making it distinct from the more ductile asthenosphere below.
 
• Its thickness varies between **40 km to 280 km**, depending on whether it is oceanic or continental lithosphere.
 
• The processes of plate tectonics, such as earthquakes and volcanic activity, occur due to the movement and interaction of lithospheric plates.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Asthenosphere**

 
 
• The asthenosphere lies below the lithosphere and is composed of semi-fluid, ductile rock.
 
• It facilitates the movement of tectonic plates by acting as a **lubricating layer**.
 
• Its depth ranges from approximately 100 km to 200 km beneath Earth's surface.
 
 
 
• **Mesosphere**
 
 
• The mesosphere refers to the part of Earth's mantle beneath the asthenosphere.
 
• It is more rigid than the asthenosphere due to higher pressure and temperature conditions.
 
 
 
• **Stratosphere**
 
 
• The stratosphere is a layer of Earth's atmosphere, not part of its solid structure.
 
• It lies above the troposphere and contains the ozone layer, which absorbs ultraviolet radiation from the sun.
 
 
 
• **Plate Tectonics**
 
 
• Plate tectonics is the study of the movement and interaction of the lithospheric plates.
 
• Major geological phenomena, such as earthquakes, mountain formation, and volcanic eruptions, are driven by these interactions.

questions.question:

• **SEWA Bank** was established in **1974** to provide financial services to poor and self-employed women.
 
• The bank was founded in **Gujarat, India**, by the Self-Employed Women's Association (SEWA).
 
• **SEWA**, a trade union of women workers in the informal sector, played a key role in the formation of this bank.
 
• The primary objective of SEWA Bank is to provide microfinance services, enabling women to gain financial independence and improve their socio-economic status.
 
• It operates as a cooperative bank, empowering self-employed women by offering savings, credit, and insurance products tailored to their needs.

• Microfinance refers to financial services provided to low-income individuals or groups who lack access to traditional banking services.
 
• It includes loans, savings accounts, insurance, and financial literacy training aimed at alleviating poverty.

• **Cooperative Banks:**
 
 
• Cooperative banks are financial institutions owned and operated by their members, focusing on mutual aid and community welfare.

• SEWA Bank has helped thousands of women improve their livelihoods by providing access to affordable credit and financial services.
 
• It serves as a model for women-centric microfinance institutions globally.

questions.question: From which country is the concept of independence of the judiciary in the Indian Constitution taken?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**United States of America**__.

*__Key Points__

__
 
• The concept of **independence of the judiciary** in the Indian Constitution is inspired by the judicial system of the **United States of America**.
 
• The USA's Constitution ensures a strong and independent judiciary through the principle of **separation of powers**, which India adopted with suitable modifications.
 
• In India, the judiciary is established as an independent organ under the Constitution, particularly in Articles **124** to **147** for the Supreme Court and Articles **214** to **231** for High Courts.
 
• The American model emphasizes the judiciary's role as the **guardian of the Constitution**, which inspired India's adoption of the power of **judicial review**.
 
• India's judiciary operates independently from the executive and legislature, ensuring **checks and balances** within the democratic framework.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Judicial Independence:**

 
 
• Judicial independence refers to the ability of courts and judges to perform their duties free from influence or interference by other branches of government or external forces.
 
• It is a cornerstone of democracy, ensuring impartiality and fairness in interpreting and enforcing laws.
 
 
 
• **Separation of Powers:**
 
 
• This principle divides the government into three branches: the legislature, executive, and judiciary.
 
• Each branch functions independently to prevent concentration of power and ensure a system of checks and balances.
 
 
 
• **Judicial Review in India:**
 
 
• Judicial review empowers courts to examine the constitutionality of legislative and executive actions.
 
• It is derived from the American precedent of Marbury v. Madison* (1803) and enshrined in Article 13 of the Indian Constitution.
 
 
 
• **Key Constitutional Provisions:**
 
 
• Article 50 of the Indian Constitution directs the state to separate the judiciary from the executive in public services.
 
• The Supreme Court of India is the apex judicial body, established under Article 124.
 
• High Courts and subordinate courts are integral parts of the judiciary, ensuring justice at various levels.

questions.question: In which Olympics did PV Sindhu win a silver medal?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**2016 Summer Olympics (Rio)**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• PV Sindhu won the **silver medal** in the women's singles badminton event at the **2016 Summer Olympics** held in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil.
 
• She became the **first Indian woman** to win an Olympic silver medal in badminton and the youngest Indian to achieve this feat at the age of **21**.
 
• In the final match, PV Sindhu competed against Spain's Carolina Marin, the then World No. 1, and secured the second position.
 
• This historic achievement made her a household name in India and brought immense recognition to Indian badminton on the global stage.
 
• Her silver medal win was instrumental in inspiring a new generation of badminton players in India.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Badminton at the Olympics:**

 
 
• Badminton was introduced in the Summer Olympics in **1992**, held in Barcelona, Spain.
 
• The five events in badminton at the Olympics are men's singles, women's singles, men's doubles, women's doubles, and mixed doubles.
 
 
 
• **India’s Achievements in Badminton:**
 
 
• India has won several Olympic medals in badminton, including a bronze medal by Saina Nehwal in 2012 and a bronze by PV Sindhu in 2020 (Tokyo).
 
• PV Sindhu remains the only Indian to have won two Olympic medals in badminton (a silver in 2016 and a bronze in 2020).
 
 
 
• **PV Sindhu’s Career Highlights:**

questions.question: Which of the following mausoleum shapes was found in the architecture of the Lodhi dynasty?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Octagonal**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The mausoleums of the Lodhi dynasty predominantly featured **octagonal shapes**, representing a unique architectural style of the era.
 
• These octagonal tombs were surrounded by gardens, showcasing the **Persian influence** in the Lodhi architectural design.
 
• The octagonal plan was often used in tomb architecture to symbolize **balance and eternity** in Islamic traditions.
 
• Prominent examples of this design include the tomb of Sikandar Lodi and Mohammed Shah, both characterized by the **octagonal chamber with domes**.
 
• This style marked a transition from the earlier Tughlaq architecture to the more refined Mughal architectural designs.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Lodhi Dynasty (1451-1526):**

 
 
• The Lodhis were the last dynasty of the Delhi Sultanate before the advent of the Mughals.
 
• They were of Afghan origin and introduced significant architectural innovations during their reign.
 
• Their architecture focused on tombs, mosques, and gardens, blending **Islamic and Persian styles**.
 
 
 
• **Significance of Tomb Architecture:**
 
 
• Tombs were designed to honor deceased rulers and symbolize their spiritual journey in the afterlife.
 
• The use of symmetry, domes, and geometric patterns reflected **Islamic cosmology and artistry.**
 
 
 
• **Persian Influence on Lodhi Architecture:**
 
 
• The Lodhis adopted **charbagh gardens** and Persian motifs in their architectural designs.
 
• The octagonal layout of tombs was inspired by Persian principles of balance and harmony.
 
 
 
• **Key Examples of Lodhi Architectural Style:**
 
 
• **Sikandar Lodi’s Tomb:** Located in the Lodhi Gardens, it is one of the finest examples of octagonal tomb architecture.
 
• **Mohammed Shah’s Tomb:** Another notable octagonal tomb surrounded by gardens, emphasizing the Persian influence.

questions.question: Name the dance form of North-West India in which dancers emulate the movements of snakes?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Kalbeliya**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Kalbeliya** is a traditional folk dance form of Rajasthan, specifically associated with the Kalbeliya tribe, who are known for their nomadic lifestyle.
 
• The dance mimics the movements of snakes and is performed with fluid and graceful movements, reflecting the tribe's expertise in snake handling.
 
• Kalbeliya dancers wear black swirling skirts adorned with intricate embroidery and silver jewelry, symbolizing their cultural heritage.
 
• Music for Kalbeliya dance is typically provided by instruments such as the **pungi** (a wind instrument), **dholak**, and **khartal**, creating rhythmic beats.
 
• In 2010, Kalbeliya dance was included in UNESCO's list of **Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity**, highlighting its cultural significance.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Kalbeliya Tribe:**

 
 
• The Kalbeliya tribe of Rajasthan historically worked as snake charmers and are deeply connected to the desert lifestyle.
 
• Their dance and music represent their close association with nature and their nomadic traditions.
 
 
 
• **Costumes in Kalbeliya Dance:**
 
 
• The dancers wear long, flowing black skirts with vibrant colors and mirror work, showcasing intricate Rajasthani artistry.
 
• Jewelry plays a significant role, with silver ornaments accentuating the dancers' movements.
 
 
 
• **Music Instruments:**
 
 
• The pungi, a wind instrument traditionally used by snake charmers, is central to the music of Kalbeliya dance.
 
• Other instruments include the dholak, a hand drum, and khartal, a wooden percussion instrument.
 
 
 
• **UNESCO Recognition:**
 
 
• Kalbeliya dance was recognized by UNESCO in 2010 as part of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.
 
• This recognition highlights the importance of preserving the cultural traditions of the Kalbeliya tribe.

questions.question: Who among the following is the fourth Chief Election Commissioner of India?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Nagendra Singh**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Nagendra Singh** served as the fourth Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) of India.
 
• He held the position from **1 October 1972 to 6 February 1973**.
 
• Nagendra Singh was known for his significant contributions to the Indian administrative and judicial systems.
 
• He later went on to serve as a judge and eventually the **President of the International Court of Justice (ICJ)** at The Hague.
 
• His tenure as CEC was relatively short, but he played a vital role in ensuring free and fair elections during his term.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) of India:**

 
 
• The CEC is the head of the Election Commission of India, responsible for administering elections to the Parliament, State Legislatures, and the offices of the President and Vice President.
 
• The CEC is appointed by the President of India and serves a tenure of six years or until the age of 65, whichever is earlier.
 
• The Election Commission is an independent constitutional authority under Article 324 of the Indian Constitution.
 
 
 
• **International Court of Justice (ICJ):**
 
 
• The ICJ, also known as the World Court, is the principal judicial organ of the United Nations.
 
• Nagendra Singh was the first Indian to serve as the President of the ICJ (1985-1988).
 
• The ICJ resolves disputes between states and gives advisory opinions on international legal issues.
 
 
 
• **Election Commission of India:**
 
 
• It was established on 25 January 1950 and is headquartered in New Delhi.
 
• It is responsible for ensuring free and fair elections in India.
 
• The commission comprises the Chief Election Commissioner and two Election Commissioners.
 
 
 
• **Role of the Chief Election Commissioner:**
 
 
• The CEC ensures the impartial conduct of elections and enforces the Model Code of Conduct.
 
• They oversee the preparation of electoral rolls and the distribution of voter identification cards.
 
• The CEC has the authority to supervise the entire electoral process in the country.

questions.question: In which of the following cases does revenue deficit occur?

options.text: When the government’s total revenue exceeds its expenditure
When the government’s revenue is added to its expenditure
When the government’s total revenue is less than its expenditure
When the government’s total revenue is equal to its expenditure

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**When the government’s total revenue is less than its expenditure**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• A revenue deficit occurs when the **government's total revenue receipts are less than its total revenue expenditure**.
 
• It indicates that the government is unable to cover its regular operational expenses through its revenue receipts.
 
• **Revenue receipts** include income from taxes (direct and indirect) and non-tax revenues like profits from public sector enterprises and dividends.
 
• **Revenue expenditure** refers to spending on day-to-day operations such as salaries, subsidies, interest payments, and administrative costs.
 
• A persistent revenue deficit is considered unhealthy for the economy as it compels the government to borrow or cut into its capital expenditures, which affects developmental activities.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Fiscal Deficit:**

 
 
• It represents the total borrowing requirements of the government.
 
• Fiscal deficit occurs when the total expenditure of the government exceeds its total receipts (excluding borrowings).
 
• A high fiscal deficit indicates excessive government borrowing, which can lead to inflation or debt issues.
 
 
 
• **Primary Deficit:**
 
 
• Primary deficit is calculated as the fiscal deficit minus interest payments on previous borrowings.
 
• It reflects the borrowing requirements of the government excluding interest obligations.
 
 
 
• **Capital Expenditure:**
 
 
• It refers to government spending on creating assets such as infrastructure, education facilities, and health services.
 
• Unlike revenue expenditure, capital expenditure contributes to long-term economic growth.
 
 
 
• **Ways to Reduce Revenue Deficit:**
 
 
• Improving tax collection efficiency and increasing tax base.
 
• Reducing unnecessary subsidies and controlling administrative costs.
 
• Encouraging privatization or monetization of government assets.

• The Khilafat Movement (1919-1924) was initiated by Indian Muslims to protest against the dismemberment of the Ottoman Empire and the abolition of the Caliphate by the British after World War I.
 
• The movement sought to preserve the authority and sanctity of the Caliph, considered the spiritual head of the global Islamic community.
 
• Key leaders of the movement included Maulana Mohammad Ali and Maulana Shaukat Ali, who were collectively known as the Ali Brothers.
 
• It was supported by Mahatma Gandhi as part of his strategy to unite Hindus and Muslims in the struggle for India's independence.
 
• The Khilafat Movement eventually declined after Mustafa Kemal Atatürk abolished the Caliphate in 1924 and established a secular government in Turkey.

• **Caliphate:**
 
 
• The Caliphate refers to a form of Islamic governance led by a Caliph, who is seen as the successor to Prophet Muhammad.
 
• The Ottoman Sultan held the title of Caliph until the abolition of the Caliphate by Mustafa Kemal Atatürk in 1924.
 
 
 
• **Non-Cooperation Movement:**
 
 
• The Khilafat Movement was closely linked to the Non-Cooperation Movement led by Mahatma Gandhi, which aimed to resist British rule through nonviolent means.
 
• The two movements created a brief period of Hindu-Muslim unity in India's struggle for independence.
 
 
 
• **Impact of the Movement:**
 
 
• Although the Khilafat Movement failed to achieve its goals, it played a significant role in mobilizing Indian Muslims against British imperialism.
 
• Its decline marked the beginning of communal tensions between Hindus and Muslims in India.

questions.question: Which of the following features conveys the meaning ‘creating equalitarian society’ ?

__
 
• **Fundamental Rights**, enshrined in Part III of the Indian Constitution, aim to protect the rights of individuals and promote equality, liberty, and dignity of all citizens.
 
• Article 14 ensures **equality before the law** and equal protection of the laws, laying the foundation for an equalitarian society.
 
• Articles 15 and 17 prohibit discrimination on grounds such as religion, race, caste, sex, or place of birth and abolish untouchability, fostering social equality.
 
• Article 23 prohibits human trafficking and forced labor, which indirectly promotes equality and safeguards the weaker sections of society.
 
• Fundamental Rights act as a safeguard against exploitation and provide an essential framework for creating an inclusive and equalitarian society in India.

• **Written Constitution**

 
 
• A written constitution provides a formal and structured document laying out the fundamental principles and framework of governance.
 
• India's Constitution is the longest written constitution in the world and reflects the diversity and complexity of Indian society.
 
 
 
• **Emergency Provisions**
 
 
• Emergency provisions, under Part XVIII of the Constitution, enable the central government to safeguard the sovereignty, unity, and integrity of the nation during crises.
 
• These provisions, however, are not directly related to creating an equalitarian society.
 
 
 
• **Federal System**
 
 
• India follows a quasi-federal system, with a strong center and autonomous states, as outlined in the Constitution.
 
• While federalism ensures decentralization of power, it does not inherently focus on creating an equalitarian society.
 
 
 
• **Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP)**
 
 
• Part IV of the Constitution contains DPSPs, which guide the state in framing policies aimed at social and economic welfare.
 
• Though not enforceable by law, DPSPs complement Fundamental Rights in striving for a just and equitable society.

questions.question:
Which of the following sets consists of only compounds?

A) Sugar solution, Calcium carbonate, Methane, Baking soda

B) Sugar, Calcium carbonate, Methane, Baking soda

C) Sugar solution, Calcium, Methane, Baking soda

D) Sugar solution, Calcium carbonate, Methane, Soda water
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**B) Sugar, Calcium carbonate, Methane, Baking soda**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• A **compound** is a substance composed of two or more elements chemically bonded in a fixed ratio.
 
• **Sugar (C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁)** is a compound made of carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen.
 
• **Calcium carbonate (CaCO₃)** is a compound containing calcium, carbon, and oxygen.
 
• **Methane (CH₄)** is a compound comprising carbon and hydrogen.
 
• **Baking soda (NaHCO₃)**, also known as sodium bicarbonate, is a compound containing sodium, hydrogen, carbon, and oxygen.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Elements:** Pure substances consisting of only one type of atom (e.g., hydrogen, oxygen).
 
• **Mixtures:** Combinations of two or more substances that are physically blended but not chemically bonded (e.g., sugar solution, soda water).
 
• **Compounds:** Formed through chemical bonding between elements, resulting in new substances with distinct properties (e.g., water, carbon dioxide).
 
• **Chemical Formula:** Represents the composition of a compound, indicating the type and number of atoms (e.g., CH₄ for methane).
 
• **Physical vs. Chemical Change:** Mixing substances (like sugar solution) is a physical change, while forming compounds involves chemical changes.

questions.question: Which article empowers the Supreme Court to exercise the jurisdiction and powers of the federal court under any pre-constitution law?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Article 135**__.

__
 
• **Article 135** of the Indian Constitution empowers the Supreme Court to exercise the jurisdiction and powers of a federal court under any pre-constitution law in certain cases.
 
• This provision ensures that the Supreme Court retains jurisdiction in matters where powers were exercised by the Federal Court of India before the Constitution came into effect.
 
• The Federal Court of India, established under the **Government of India Act, 1935**, was a precursor to the Supreme Court of India.
 
• Article 135 allows the Supreme Court to hear cases related to pre-constitutional laws until they are repealed or amended by Parliament.
 
• This article plays a crucial role in ensuring continuity and stability in India’s legal framework during the transition from colonial to independent governance.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Federal Court of India (1937-1950):**

 
 
• It was established under the Government of India Act, 1935, to resolve disputes between provinces and hear appeals against decisions of the High Courts.
 
• The Federal Court was replaced by the Supreme Court of India upon the adoption of the Constitution in 1950.
 
 
 
• **Government of India Act, 1935:**
 
 
• It was a significant constitutional reform by the British Parliament that served as a blueprint for India’s federal structure.
 
• It introduced provincial autonomy and a federal court system in British India.
 
 
 
• **Jurisdiction of the Supreme Court:**
 
 
• The Supreme Court has original, appellate, and advisory jurisdiction under Articles 131-136 and Article 143 of the Constitution.
 
• Article 135 complements these powers by extending the Court’s jurisdiction over pre-constitutional legal matters.
 
 
 
• **Continuity of Legal Framework:**
 
 
• Article 372 of the Constitution also ensures that laws in force before the adoption of the Constitution continue unless repealed or amended.
 
• In combination with Article 135, this ensures seamless legal continuity during India’s transition to constitutional democracy.

questions.question: Which hymn from the Rigveda was used by the Brahmanas of ancient India to justify the Varna system?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Purusha Sukta**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The **Purusha Sukta**, found in the 10th Mandala of the Rigveda, is a hymn that describes the cosmic being (Purusha) as the source of all creation.
 
• This hymn is significant as it outlines the **origin of the Varna system** in ancient India, associating each Varna with a body part of Purusha.
 
• According to the hymn, the **Brahmins** (priests) emerged from Purusha's mouth, the **Kshatriyas** (warriors) from his arms, the **Vaishyas** (traders) from his thighs, and the **Shudras** (laborers) from his feet.
 
• The Purusha Sukta was later interpreted by the Brahmanas to justify the **hierarchical Varna system** as a divine and immutable social structure.
 
• It is one of the earliest references to the concept of societal division based on occupational roles and duties in ancient Indian texts.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Varna System**

 
 
• The Varna system classified society into four groups: Brahmins, Kshatriyas, Vaishyas, and Shudras, based on their roles in society.
 
• This division was initially flexible and based on one's profession and abilities, but over time, it became hereditary and rigid.
 
• The system formed the basis of India's caste hierarchy, which influenced social, economic, and political life for centuries.
 
 
 
• **Purusha**
 
 
• The term "Purusha" in the Rigveda refers to the cosmic being or universal spirit that encompasses and transcends all of creation.
 
• The sacrifice of Purusha in the Purusha Sukta symbolizes the creation of the universe and the establishment of order in society.
 
 
 
• **Rigveda**
 
 
• The Rigveda is the oldest of the four Vedas and is composed of over 1,000 hymns dedicated to various deities.
 
• It is a foundational text of Hinduism and provides insights into the early Vedic civilization.
 
 
 
• **Brahmanas**
 
 
• The Brahmanas are a collection of prose texts attached to the Vedas, providing explanations of rituals and hymns.
 
• They played a crucial role in the interpretation and justification of social and religious practices, including the Varna system.

questions.question: IR-8 is a dwarf variety of which crop?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Rice**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **IR-8** is a high-yielding dwarf variety of rice developed by the International Rice Research Institute (IRRI) in the Philippines in 1966.
 
• It is referred to as the "Miracle Rice" for its ability to significantly increase rice production and address food shortages in developing nations.
 
• IR-8 was developed through crossbreeding techniques using rice varieties from Indonesia and China.
 
• This variety is characterized by its short stature, which prevents lodging (falling over) during heavy rains or strong winds, a common problem for traditional tall rice varieties.
 
• IR-8 played a crucial role in the Green Revolution, particularly in Asia, helping many countries achieve self-sufficiency in rice production.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **International Rice Research Institute (IRRI)**

 
 
• IRRI, based in Los Baños, Philippines, is the world's premier research organization dedicated to rice science.
 
• Founded in 1960, IRRI focuses on improving rice production and ensuring global food security.
 
• It collaborates with governments, agricultural organizations, and farmers to develop sustainable rice varieties and farming practices.
 
 
 
• **Green Revolution**
 
 
• The Green Revolution refers to a period of agricultural transformation during the mid-20th century, aimed at increasing food production worldwide.
 
• It involved the development of high-yielding crop varieties, including IR-8, along with the use of chemical fertilizers and advanced irrigation techniques.
 
• The Green Revolution helped countries like India and the Philippines overcome chronic food shortages.
 
 
 
• **Lodging in Crops**
 
 
• Lodging occurs when crop plants fall over due to heavy rains, strong winds, or their own weight.
 
• Dwarf varieties like IR-8 minimize lodging due to their shorter and sturdier stems.
 
• This feature is critical for ensuring consistent yields in regions prone to adverse weather conditions.
 
 
 
• **Impact of IR-8**
 
 
• IR-8 had a transformational impact on rice production in Asia, particularly in countries like India, Indonesia, and the Philippines.
 
• Its high yield potential helped reduce hunger and malnutrition in regions heavily reliant on rice as a staple food.
 
• It paved the way for further research and development of improved rice varieties worldwide.

questions.question: The Olympic Games was organised in Asia for the first time in ____________.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**1964**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The first Olympic Games held in Asia were the **1964 Summer Olympics in Tokyo, Japan**.
 
• The 1964 Tokyo Olympics were significant as they marked **Asia's debut as a host continent** for the modern Olympic Games.
 
• Tokyo was originally scheduled to host the 1940 Olympics, but they were canceled due to World War II.
 
• These games were the first to be broadcast internationally via satellite, showcasing a new era of global sports broadcasting.
 
• The 1964 Olympics featured **new technological advancements**, such as the introduction of synthetic running tracks and the use of computers for timing and scoring.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Olympic Games Background:**

 
 
• The modern Olympic Games were first held in Athens, Greece, in 1896.
 
• The Olympics occur every four years and feature summer and winter editions.
 
• The International Olympic Committee (IOC), founded in 1894, oversees the organization of the Games.
 
 
 
• **Tokyo 1964 Key Highlights:**
 
 
• Japan emerged as a global power post-World War II, using the Olympics to symbolize its recovery and modernization.
 
• Judo and volleyball were introduced as official Olympic sports for the first time.
 
• The iconic Shinkansen (bullet train) was launched in conjunction with the games to improve infrastructure.
 
 
 
• **Asia’s Later Olympics:**
 
 
• After 1964, Asia hosted other Olympics, including Seoul 1988 (South Korea), Beijing 2008 (China), and Tokyo 2020 (delayed to 2021 due to COVID-19).
 
• The Winter Olympics were also hosted in Asia, including Sapporo 1972 and PyeongChang 2018.
 
 
 
• **Significance of Tokyo’s Hosting:**
 
 
• Tokyo's hosting marked Asia's emergence as a key player in international sports.
 
• It showcased Japan's technological and economic resurgence post-war.
 
• The games emphasized global unity, peace, and progress during the Cold War era.

questions.question: The Chandela dynasty of Rajput clan ruled which of the following regions between 9th and 13th century in early medieval period of India?

__
 
• The Chandela dynasty, belonging to the Rajput clan, ruled the region of **Bundelkhand** in present-day Madhya Pradesh and Uttar Pradesh during the 9th to 13th century CE.
 
• The Chandelas are renowned for their significant contributions to architecture, particularly the **Khajuraho group of temples**, which are UNESCO World Heritage Sites.
 
• They ruled from their capital at **Khajuraho** and later at Mahoba, showcasing their administrative and cultural prowess.
 
• The Chandela rulers were initially vassals of the Pratiharas but later established their independent rule in the region.
 
• Key rulers of the dynasty include **Yashovarman** and **Dhangadeva**, who were instrumental in expanding and consolidating the Chandela kingdom.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Bundelkhand Region:**

 
 
• Bundelkhand spans parts of present-day Madhya Pradesh and Uttar Pradesh in central India.
 
• The region is known for its rugged terrain and historical significance in Indian history.
 
 
 
• **Khajuraho Temples:**
 
 
• Built by the Chandela rulers, these temples are known for their intricate carvings and sculptures representing various aspects of life, spirituality, and art.
 
• The temples primarily belong to the Hindu and Jain traditions, reflecting the religious harmony of the era.
 
 
 
• **Chandela Dynasty Highlights:**
 
 
• The Chandelas were patrons of art and architecture, leaving behind an enduring legacy through their monuments.
 
• Their rule was marked by a blend of military strength and cultural achievements.

• The dynasty declined after the 13th century due to invasions by the Delhi Sultanate and internal conflicts.
 
• Despite their decline, the Chandelas left an indelible mark on Indian history through their contributions to art and architecture.

questions.question: Who among the following started the ‘Shuddhi Movement’ to bring back converted Hindus to the main Hindu society?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Swami Dayanand**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The **Shuddhi Movement** was started by Swami Dayanand Saraswati, the founder of the Arya Samaj, in the late 19th century.
 
• It aimed to **reconvert individuals**, primarily Hindus who had converted to other religions, back to Hinduism.
 
• The movement emphasized the **purification and return** of individuals to the Vedic fold, which Swami Dayanand considered the original and pure form of Hinduism.
 
• Swami Dayanand’s teachings were rooted in the principles of the **Vedas**, which he considered infallible and the ultimate source of knowledge.
 
• The Shuddhi Movement also aimed to **eradicate caste distinctions** and unify Hindu society under a common Vedic culture.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Arya Samaj**

 
 
• Founded by Swami Dayanand Saraswati in 1875, Arya Samaj promoted the idea of returning to the teachings of the Vedas.
 
• It advocated social reforms such as the abolition of caste discrimination, child marriage, and idol worship.
 
• The Arya Samaj emphasized education, especially for women, and the upliftment of society through Vedic teachings.
 
 
 
• **Swami Dayanand Saraswati**
 
 
• Born in 1824 in Tankara, Gujarat, he was a reformer and religious leader who criticized ritualistic practices and superstitions in Hinduism.
 
• His motto was "Back to the Vedas," emphasizing the revival of Vedic knowledge and practices.
 
• He authored the book **Satyarth Prakash**, which outlined his reformist ideas and principles.
 
 
 
• **Vedas**
 
 
• The Vedas are the oldest sacred texts of Hinduism, consisting of four main collections: Rigveda, Yajurveda, Samaveda, and Atharvaveda.
 
• Swami Dayanand believed the Vedas were divinely revealed and contained the ultimate truth.
 
• The Shuddhi Movement sought to reconnect people with these ancient texts and their teachings.
 
 
 
• **Religious Conversion in India**
 
 
• The Shuddhi Movement was a response to mass conversions to Islam and Christianity during the colonial era.
 
• It aimed to restore the cultural and religious identity of Hindus who had converted.
 
• The movement also addressed social issues by advocating unity among Hindus and reducing caste divisions.

questions.question: Who among the following was chosen by Gandhiji as the first Satyagrahi of the individual Satyagraha movement?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Acharya Vinoba Bhave**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Acharya Vinoba Bhave was chosen by Mahatma Gandhi as the first Satyagrahi for the Individual Satyagraha movement in **October 1940**.
 
• The Individual Satyagraha was launched as a protest against British policies and the **restrictions on freedom of expression during World War II**.
 
• Vinoba Bhave’s selection highlighted his commitment to Gandhian principles and his reputation as a spiritual leader and social reformer.
 
• The Individual Satyagraha emphasized the principle of non-violence and was intended to express **India’s right to speak truthfully against injustice**.
 
• After Vinoba Bhave, the second Satyagrahi chosen by Gandhiji was **Jawaharlal Nehru**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Individual Satyagraha Movement:**

 
 
• It was launched in 1940 after the failure of negotiations between the Indian National Congress and the British government regarding **India’s participation in World War II**.
 
• The movement was characterized by non-violent protest against British rule and the **repressive Defence of India Act**.
 
• Unlike mass movements, Individual Satyagraha was carried out by individuals in a symbolic manner to avoid large-scale repression.
 
 
 
• **Vinoba Bhave:**
 
 
• Vinoba Bhave was a prominent Gandhian leader, philosopher, and social reformer known for his **Bhoodan Movement**, which aimed at land redistribution.
 
• He was deeply influenced by Gandhian principles of **truth, non-violence, and self-reliance**.
 
 
 
• **World War II and Indian Nationalism:**
 
 
• During World War II, the British government’s unilateral decision to involve India in the war without consultation with Indian leaders led to widespread resentment.
 
• This period marked the intensification of India’s struggle for independence and the rise of movements like **Individual Satyagraha**.
 
 
 
• **Defence of India Act:**
 
 
• This act was introduced by the British government in 1939 to suppress dissent and maintain control during World War II.
 
• It was criticized for **violating civil liberties** and enabling arbitrary arrests and censorship.

questions.question: Who among the following chroniclers wrote his first chronicle in 1356?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Ziyauddin Barani**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Ziyauddin Barani** was a notable chronicler and historian of the Delhi Sultanate period in India.
 
• He wrote his first chronicle, **"Tarikh-i-Firoz Shahi"**, in 1356, which documented the history of the Delhi Sultanate.
 
• Barani served as a court historian under Sultan Muhammad bin Tughlaq and later under Firuz Shah Tughlaq.
 
• His writings reflect his Islamic perspective and provide valuable insights into the political, social, and economic aspects of the Delhi Sultanate.
 
• Barani emphasized the importance of Islamic governance and the role of religion in statecraft, often critiquing rulers for their deviation from Islamic principles.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Tarikh-i-Firoz Shahi**

 
 
• This work is an essential source for understanding the Delhi Sultanate's history during the 13th and 14th centuries.
 
• It covers the reigns of rulers such as Ghiyasuddin Balban, Alauddin Khilji, and Muhammad bin Tughlaq.
 
• Barani’s chronicle provides detailed accounts of administration, military campaigns, and societal developments.
 
 
 
• **Minhaj-us-Siraj**
 
 
• An earlier historian who wrote **"Tabaqat-i-Nasiri"**, covering the history of Islamic rule in India up to 1260.
 
• His work is considered one of the most authentic sources for the early Delhi Sultanate period.
 
 
 
• **Al-Biruni**
 
 
• A renowned Persian scholar, Al-Biruni authored **"Kitab al-Hind"**, which focused on Indian culture, sciences, and religion during the early 11th century.
 
• He was associated with Mahmud of Ghazni and visited India during his invasions.
 
 
 
• **Ibn Sina (Avicenna)**
 
 
• A prominent Persian polymath known for his works on medicine, philosophy, and science, such as **"The Canon of Medicine."**
 
• His contributions were unrelated to the chronicle tradition of Indian history.

questions.question: Deba Prasad Das, Pankaj Charan Das and Gangadhar Pradhan were the famous exponents of which of the following dance forms?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Odissi**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Deba Prasad Das, Pankaj Charan Das, and Gangadhar Pradhan are celebrated exponents of **Odissi**, one of the eight classical dance forms of India.
 
• Odissi originated from the state of **Odisha** and is known for its fluid movements, grace, and intricate expressions (abhinaya).
 
• Deba Prasad Das and Pankaj Charan Das contributed significantly to reviving the traditional dance form post-independence, focusing on its **ritualistic roots in temples.**
 
• Gangadhar Pradhan was instrumental in promoting Odissi globally and founded the **Orissa Dance Academy** to train future generations in this art form.
 
• Odissi performances often depict themes from Hindu mythology, especially stories of Lord **Jagannath, Krishna, and Radha**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Odissi Dance Characteristics:**

 
 
• Odissi is characterized by **tribhanga (three-bend posture)** and the **Chowka (square stance),** which form the foundation of its movements.
 
• The dance is accompanied by **Odissi music,** which is a blend of classical and folk traditions originating from Odisha.
 
• The **ghungroo** (ankle bells) worn by dancers accentuate the rhythm of foot movements.
 
 
 
• **Historical Context:**
 
 
• Odissi traces its roots back to **Natya Shastra,** an ancient Sanskrit text on performing arts written by Bharat Muni.
 
• The dance was traditionally performed by **Maharis** (temple dancers) as an offering to deities in temples, particularly Lord Jagannath's temple in Puri.
 
 
 
• **Other Classical Dance Forms of India:**
 
 
• **Bharatanatyam:** Originated in Tamil Nadu, known for its fixed upper torso and intricate footwork.
 
• **Kathak:** Originated in northern India, characterized by storytelling through expressive gestures and swift spins.
 
• **Manipuri:** Originated in Manipur, focusing on soft, graceful movements depicting themes of Lord Krishna.
 
• **Sattriya:** Originated in Assam, performed in monasteries (Satras) as a form of devotional art.
 
 
 
• **Global Recognition:**
 
 
• Odissi has gained global acclaim for its aesthetic appeal and storytelling, often performed at international cultural festivals.
 
• Efforts by institutions and dancers like Gangadhar Pradhan have contributed to its recognition as a UNESCO **Intangible Cultural Heritage.**

questions.question: The deficiency of iodine causes _________.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Goitre**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Goitre is a condition characterized by the abnormal enlargement of the thyroid gland.
 
• The primary cause of goitre is a deficiency of iodine, a vital mineral required for producing thyroid hormones.
 
• Thyroid hormones (thyroxine and triiodothyronine) regulate metabolism, growth, and development in the body.
 
• Iodine deficiency disrupts hormone production, leading to the thyroid gland's overcompensation and subsequent enlargement.
 
• Goitre is commonly observed in regions where iodine levels in soil and water are low, leading to insufficient dietary intake.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Iodine:**

 
 
• Iodine is an essential micronutrient required for the synthesis of thyroid hormones.
 
• It is naturally present in foods such as seafood, dairy products, and iodized salt.
 
 
 
• **Thyroid Gland:**
 
 
• The thyroid gland is a butterfly-shaped organ located at the base of the neck.
 
• It plays a key role in regulating metabolism, heart rate, and body temperature.
 
 
 
• **Other Iodine Deficiency Disorders (IDD):**
 
 
• Cretinism: A severe form of hypothyroidism in infants due to iodine deficiency during pregnancy.
 
• Hypothyroidism: A condition where the thyroid gland produces insufficient thyroid hormones.
 
 
 
• **Prevention:**
 
 
• The most effective way to prevent iodine deficiency is the consumption of iodized salt.
 
• National programs for universal salt iodization have significantly reduced iodine deficiency globally.

questions.question: By which of the following authors is the English novel ‘Three Men in a Boat’ written?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Jerome K Jerome**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Three Men in a Boat** is an English comic novel written by Jerome K Jerome, first published in 1889.
 
• The novel narrates a humorous account of a boating holiday taken by three friends—Jerome, George, and Harris—along with the dog Montmorency on the River Thames.
 
• Originally intended as a guidebook for Thames River travelers, the book is noted for its witty humor and timeless appeal.
 
• The novel was an instant success upon its release and continues to be regarded as one of the classics of English literature.
 
• Jerome K Jerome wrote the book in a semi-autobiographical style, drawing on his own experiences and observations.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Jerome K Jerome:**

 
 
• Born on May 2, 1859, in Walsall, England, Jerome Klapka Jerome was a prolific English author and humorist.
 
• Apart from "Three Men in a Boat," his other notable works include "Idle Thoughts of an Idle Fellow" and "Three Men on the Bummel."
 
• He was known for his sharp wit, observational humor, and engaging writing style.
 
 
 
• **Comic Novel Genre:**
 
 
• A comic novel is a literary genre that uses humor as a central element to engage readers.
 
• It often includes satire, irony, and exaggeration to critique social norms or human behavior.
 
 
 
• **River Thames:**
 
 
• The River Thames is the longest river entirely in England, flowing through London and several historical landmarks.
 
• It has been a source of inspiration for numerous literary works, including "Three Men in a Boat."
 
 
 
• **Legacy of the Novel:**
 
 
• "Three Men in a Boat" has been adapted into several films, television shows, and theatrical productions.
 
• Its humor and relatability have ensured its popularity across generations and cultures.

questions.question: According to the Human Development Report 2021-22, what is the percentage share of health deprivation in India's overall multidimensional poverty?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Option 3 (31.9%)**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• According to the **Human Development Report (HDR) 2021-22**, India's overall Multidimensional Poverty Index (MPI) indicates that **31.9% of the deprivation is attributed to health**.
 
• Health deprivation in MPI is measured by indicators such as **nutrition, child mortality, and access to healthcare services**.
 
• The MPI for India captures various dimensions of poverty beyond income, including **education, standard of living, and health.**
 
• The report highlights that improving health services and nutrition is critical to reducing multidimensional poverty in India.
 
• The data helps policymakers to identify and address critical areas requiring intervention to improve human development outcomes.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Multidimensional Poverty Index (MPI):**

 
 
• The MPI is a measure developed by the **United Nations Development Programme (UNDP)** and the **Oxford Poverty and Human Development Initiative (OPHI)**.
 
• It captures poverty across three dimensions: **health, education, and standard of living**, using 10 indicators.
 
• Each individual in a household is classified as multidimensionally poor if they are deprived in at least 33.3% of the weighted indicators.
 
 
 
• **Health Deprivation Indicators in MPI:**
 
 
• **Nutrition:** At least one member of the household is undernourished.
 
• **Child Mortality:** A child has died in the family within the past five years.
 
 
 
• **India’s Performance in HDR 2021-22:**
 
 
• India ranked **132 out of 191 countries** in the Human Development Index (HDI).
 
• The MPI shows significant regional disparities, with rural areas and specific states contributing more to multidimensional poverty.
 
 
 
• **Steps to Address Health Deprivation:**
 
 
• Government schemes like **Ayushman Bharat**, **POSHAN Abhiyaan**, and **National Health Mission** aim to improve health indicators.
 
• Focus on access to quality healthcare, nutrition, and maternal-child health is critical to reducing health deprivation.

questions.question: Which of the following was the revenue collecting officer (collector general of revenue) in the Mauryan administration?
questions.solution:

__
 
• In the Mauryan administration, **Samaharta** was the officer responsible for collecting revenue and taxes.
 
• The term "Samaharta" translates to "collector general of revenue," focusing on ensuring proper taxation and resource management.
 
• Samaharta oversaw the collection of various taxes, including land revenue, trade taxes, and other levies under the Mauryan empire.
 
• This position was essential for maintaining the financial stability of the Mauryan administration and supporting its vast bureaucracy and army.
 
• Revenue collected by the Samaharta contributed significantly to the empire's central treasury, managed by another officer known as the **Sannidhata**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

• **Amatya:** Amatyas were high-ranking officials who acted as ministers or advisors to the king in the Mauryan administrative hierarchy.
 
• **Revenue System:** The Mauryan empire had a well-organized revenue system, including taxes on agriculture, trade, and professions, which were crucial for sustaining the vast empire.

questions.question: The English novel ‘The Rainbow’ was written by which of the following authors?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**D. H. Lawrence**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **D. H. Lawrence** wrote *The Rainbow*, which was first published in 1915.
 
• The novel explores themes of **sexuality, individualism, and relationships** within three generations of the Brangwen family in England.
 
• Upon its release, *The Rainbow* faced censorship due to its **explicit discussion of sexuality** and was banned under the Obscene Publications Act in Britain.
 
• The book is considered a landmark in English literature for its **psychological depth** and its critique of industrial society.
 
• *The Rainbow* was succeeded by a sequel, ***Women in Love*** (1920), which continues the story of the Brangwen family.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **About D. H. Lawrence:**

 
 
• David Herbert Lawrence (1885–1930) was an English novelist, poet, and essayist renowned for his exploration of human emotions and relationships.
 
• His works often challenged societal norms, particularly regarding sexuality and industrialism.
 
• Some of his other notable works include *Sons and Lovers* (1913), *Women in Love* (1920), and *Lady Chatterley's Lover* (1928).
 
 
 
• **The Rainbow's Controversy:**
 
 
• The novel was banned shortly after publication for its depiction of sexual relationships, which was deemed obscene at the time.
 
• It wasn't until the mid-20th century that *The Rainbow* gained recognition as a modern literary classic.
 
 
 
• **Industrialism in Lawrence's Works:**
 
 
• Lawrence frequently critiqued the impact of industrialization on human relationships and spirituality.
 
• In *The Rainbow*, the tension between rural traditions and industrial progress is a recurring theme.
 
 
 
• **The Sequel: *Women in Love***
 
 
• *Women in Love* follows the lives of Ursula and Gudrun Brangwen, exploring their romantic relationships and personal struggles.
 
• It is often studied alongside *The Rainbow* as part of a larger narrative examining love, individuality, and societal constraints.

questions.question: As per Livestock Census of India 2019, which of the following categories of livestock has recorded the highest population?

__

• **Livestock Census**

questions.question: Which of the following was first introduced in bacterial cells by the American molecular biologist Joshua Lederberg in 1952?

__
 
• Joshua Lederberg, an American molecular biologist, first introduced the concept of **plasmids** in bacterial cells in 1952.
 
• A plasmid is a small, circular, double-stranded DNA molecule that is distinct from the chromosomal DNA and can replicate independently.
 
• Plasmids are primarily found in bacteria but can also exist in archaea and eukaryotic organisms under certain conditions.
 
• Lederberg's discovery played a crucial role in understanding bacterial genetics and paved the way for genetic engineering techniques.
 
• Plasmids are widely used in molecular biology as vectors to clone, transfer, and manipulate genes in research and biotechnology.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Plasmid Types:**

 
 
• **F-plasmids:** Responsible for bacterial conjugation, facilitating gene transfer between cells.
 
• **R-plasmids:** Carry antibiotic resistance genes, contributing to antimicrobial resistance.
 
• **Col-plasmids:** Encode bacteriocins, proteins that kill or inhibit other bacteria.
 
• **Degradative plasmids:** Allow bacteria to metabolize unusual substances like hydrocarbons.
 
 
 
• **Significance in Biotechnology:**
 
 
• Plasmids are used as **vectors** to introduce foreign DNA into host cells in genetic engineering.
 
• They are essential in producing recombinant proteins, such as insulin and vaccines.
 
 
 
• **Bacterial Conjugation:**
 
 
• It is a process where genetic material is transferred between bacterial cells via direct contact.
 
• Plasmids play a key role in this process, enhancing genetic diversity.
 
 
 
• **Plasmid Replication:**
 
 
• Plasmids replicate independently of chromosomal DNA, either through a rolling-circle mechanism or bidirectional replication.
 
• This property makes them suitable for laboratory manipulation and cloning experiments.

questions.question: Mumbai’s famous Gateway of India was built in the memory of which British emperor's first arrival in India?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**King George V**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Gateway of India, located in Mumbai, was built to commemorate the first visit of **King George V and Queen Mary** to India in December 1911.
 
• The foundation stone of the Gateway of India was laid on **March 31, 1913**, and the structure was completed in 1924.
 
• The monument is designed in the **Indo-Saracenic architectural style**, blending elements of Hindu and Muslim architecture with European influences.
 
• It served as a ceremonial entry point for British viceroys and governors entering India and symbolized British power during colonial rule.
 
• The Gateway of India is now a prominent tourist attraction and historical landmark in Mumbai.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **King George V**:

 
 
• King George V was the Emperor of India from 1910 to 1936 as part of the British colonial rule.
 
• He was the first reigning British monarch to visit India, marking a significant event in colonial history.
 
• The visit culminated in the **Delhi Durbar of 1911**, where George V was formally proclaimed Emperor of India.
 
 
 
• **Indo-Saracenic Architecture**:
 
 
• A style of architecture prominent during the British Raj, combining Indian, Islamic, and Western architectural elements.
 
• Famous examples include the Gateway of India, Victoria Memorial in Kolkata, and Madras High Court.
 
 
 
• **Significance of the Gateway of India**:
 
 
• It was the departure point for the last British troops in India in 1948, symbolizing the end of British rule.
 
• It is now a popular site for cultural events, photography, and tourism in Mumbai.
 
 
 
• **Queen Mary**:
 
 
• Queen Mary accompanied King George V on his visit to India in 1911.
 
• She played a significant role in representing the British monarchy during the colonial period.

questions.question: Habeas Corpus is the writ issued by the Court to bring before a court _________.

options.text: a person to perform his legal duty
a tribunal from doing something in excess
a person who occupies a public office

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**a person from illegal custody**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Habeas Corpus** is a Latin term meaning "you may have the body." It is a fundamental right guaranteed under Article 32 and Article 226 of the Indian Constitution.
 
• This writ is issued to ensure that a person is not detained unlawfully or without proper justification.
 
• The primary purpose of the writ is to safeguard an individual’s liberty from illegal detention or imprisonment.
 
• The Supreme Court or High Courts can issue this writ to bring a person in illegal custody before the court to determine whether the detention is lawful.
 
• This writ is considered a vital tool in protecting the fundamental right to personal liberty under Article 21 of the Indian Constitution.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Other Types of Writs in India:**

 
 
• **Mandamus:** Issued to compel a public official, government, or lower court to perform a legal duty they have failed to perform.
 
• **Prohibition:** Issued to prevent a lower court or tribunal from exceeding its jurisdiction or acting contrary to the law.
 
• **Certiorari:** Issued to quash an order or decision of a lower court or tribunal that exceeds its jurisdiction.
 
• **Quo Warranto:** Issued to inquire into the legality of a claim to a public office.
 
 
 
• **Article 32:** Known as the "Right to Constitutional Remedies," it empowers individuals to directly approach the Supreme Court for the enforcement of fundamental rights.
 
• **Article 226:** Empowers High Courts to issue writs for the enforcement of fundamental rights and for any other purpose.
 
• **Global Perspective:** Habeas Corpus is recognized internationally and is a cornerstone of legal systems in democratic countries, ensuring protection against unlawful detention.
 
• **Historical Context:** The concept of Habeas Corpus originated in England and was formalized in the Magna Carta (1215) to protect individuals from arbitrary detention by the monarchy.

questions.question: ________ refers to relaxation of government restrictions.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Liberalisation**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Liberalisation** refers to the relaxation or removal of government restrictions and regulations in areas like trade, investment, and industries.
 
• It typically aims to encourage private sector participation, enhance competition, and improve economic efficiency.
 
• The process of liberalisation gained momentum in India with the **1991 Economic Reforms**, which marked a significant shift towards a market-driven economy.
 
• Key reforms under liberalisation include reductions in import tariffs, deregulation of industries, and easing restrictions on foreign investments.
 
• The goal of liberalisation is to foster economic growth, attract foreign investments, and integrate the domestic economy with the global market.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Privatisation:**

 
 
• Privatisation refers to the transfer of ownership, management, or control of government-owned enterprises to the private sector.
 
• It is aimed at improving efficiency, profitability, and performance of these enterprises.
 
• Examples in India include disinvestment in Air India and Bharat Petroleum Corporation Limited (BPCL).
 
 
 
• **Globalisation:**
 
 
• Globalisation refers to the integration of economies, societies, and cultures through trade, investment, technology, and information flows.
 
• It has led to increased interdependence among nations and a more interconnected global economy.
 
 
 
• **Disinvestment:**
 
 
• Disinvestment involves selling or liquidating government-owned assets or shares in public sector enterprises.
 
• The goal is to reduce the fiscal burden, improve efficiency, and promote public-private partnerships.
 
 
 
• **India’s 1991 Economic Reforms:**
 
 
• India faced a severe balance of payments crisis in 1991, prompting economic reforms under the leadership of then-Finance Minister Manmohan Singh.
 
• The reforms were based on the principles of liberalisation, privatisation, and globalisation (LPG model).
 
• They included measures like devaluation of the Indian rupee, tax reforms, and opening up of various sectors to foreign investments.

questions.question: Which of the following Articles of the Indian Constitution declares that all laws that are inconsistent with or in derogation of the Fundamental Rights shall be void?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Article 13**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Article 13 of the Indian Constitution ensures the supremacy of Fundamental Rights by declaring that any law inconsistent with or derogating from Fundamental Rights shall be void.
 
• The term "law" under Article 13 includes ordinances, orders, bye-laws, rules, regulations, notifications, customs, or usages having the force of law.
 
• Article 13 applies to both pre-Constitution laws (laws existing before January 26, 1950) and post-Constitution laws.
 
• This Article empowers courts to review legislation and strike down laws that violate Fundamental Rights.
 
• It serves as the cornerstone of judicial review in India, a crucial tool for protecting citizens' rights from unconstitutional actions.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Fundamental Rights:**

 
 
• These are enshrined in Part III of the Constitution and guarantee civil liberties to all citizens.
 
• They include rights like equality, freedom, protection against exploitation, freedom of religion, cultural and educational rights, and constitutional remedies.
 
• Fundamental Rights are enforceable by the courts, providing a mechanism for citizens to challenge violations.
 
 
 
• **Judicial Review:**
 
 
• Judicial Review refers to the power of the judiciary to examine the constitutionality of legislative acts and executive orders.
 
• Article 13 is a foundational provision enabling judicial review in India.
 
• It ensures that laws inconsistent with Fundamental Rights are invalidated, safeguarding citizens' rights.
 
 
 
• **Pre-Constitution and Post-Constitution Laws:**
 
 
• Article 13(1) deals with pre-Constitution laws, declaring them void if inconsistent with Fundamental Rights.
 
• Article 13(2) prohibits the state from making laws that infringe on Fundamental Rights.
 
 
 
• **Doctrine of Severability:**
 
 
• Under Article 13, if a part of a law violates Fundamental Rights, only that part is declared invalid.
 
• The remaining provisions of the law continue to be enforceable, provided they are separable and do not contradict the Constitution.
 
 
 
• **Doctrine of Eclipse:**
 
 
• Pre-Constitution laws inconsistent with Fundamental Rights are not entirely void; they are dormant and overshadowed by the Constitution.
 
• If the inconsistency is removed, the law can become operative again.
